title: ⭐⭐ Practice: offers, one negative, and two things moving at once

questions.prompt: A volunteer is walking round the reading room of a club in Gafsa with a tray in her hands. She is offering, not asking for information. Which sentence does she say?

options.text: Do you want any mint tea or not?
Would you like some mint tea?
Would you like any mint tea?
Do you like some mint tea in general?

questions.explanation: "Would you like some mint tea?" is what she says: a question that is really an offer or an invitation takes some, because the speaker is not asking whether the thing exists, she is expecting yes. "Would you like any mint tea?" is the trap, and it is a question in form only; any asks whether such a thing is to be had anywhere, which is not what a person holding a tray means. "Do you want any mint tea or not?" turns the offer into a demand for information, and the added or not makes it blunt rather than polite. And "Do you like some mint tea in general?" changes the verb: do you like asks about her tastes over her whole life, not about the cup being held out to her now.

questions.prompt: Wassim wrote this line in his account of the evening: "I arrived at eight and I didn't see nobody in the corridor." The line carries one negative too many. Which correction keeps his meaning and is correct English?

options.text: I didn't see anybody in the corridor.
I didn't saw anybody in the corridor.
I saw not anybody in the corridor.
I don't see nobody in the corridor.

questions.explanation: "I didn't see anybody in the corridor." repairs the line the right way: English marks a negative once, so the negative stays in the verb, didn't, and the word after it takes the any- form. The other repair would have been to leave the verb affirmative and put the negative in the word, I saw nobody, but a sentence may do one or the other, never both. "I didn't saw anybody in the corridor." fixes the double negative and creates a new mistake: didn't already carries the past, so the verb goes back to its base form, see. "I saw not anybody in the corridor." puts not straight after a full verb, a place English does not give it; a full verb takes its negative through do. And "I don't see nobody in the corridor." keeps the double negative and, on top of it, turns a finished evening into the present.

questions.prompt: A librarian in Kairouan explains her opening hours like this: "When a reading room stays open late, more pupils come to it." She now wants to say the same thing as a rule, in a single sentence built on two comparatives. Which sentence says it?

options.text: The more late a reading room stays open, the more pupils come.
The latest a reading room stays open, the most pupils come to it.
Later a reading room stays open, more pupils come to it.
The later a reading room stays open, the more pupils come to it.

questions.explanation: "The later a reading room stays open, the more pupils come to it." is the rule she wants: two halves, each opening with the and each carrying a comparative, which is exactly how English ties two movements together. "The more late a reading room stays open, the more pupils come." marks the first comparative twice over, since late is short and builds its comparative with -er. "The latest a reading room stays open, the most pupils come to it." uses two superlatives, and a superlative ranks one item above all the others instead of linking two changes. And "Later a reading room stays open, more pupils come to it." drops both the, which are the two words that hold the halves together; without them the sentence falls into two loose pieces.

questions.prompt: A small record company in Sfax stopped answering a young group's calls and quietly took its songs off every list it publishes. Which verb of the lesson names what the company did to the group?

options.text: blamed
released
shunned
surpassed

questions.explanation: "shunned" is the verb: to shun somebody or something is to keep away from it on purpose, which is what a company does when it stops answering and removes the names from its lists. "blamed" would mean it said out loud that the group was responsible for something bad, and the point of the scene is that nothing was said at all. "released" is the opposite move: to release a record is to put it on sale. And "surpassed" means went beyond, did better than, so it needs a figure or a rival being beaten, not a group being avoided.

questions.prompt: Three of these four sentences use "some" or "any" as English requires. Which one does not?

options.text: We asked the shopkeeper, but he didn't have some batteries left.
There was hardly any light left in the reading room.
I doubt whether there is any tape left in that box.
If you find any old records in the attic, keep them for the club.

questions.explanation: "We asked the shopkeeper, but he didn't have some batteries left." is the wrong one: it puts some after a negative verb, where English takes any, so the line should read he didn't have any batteries left. Each of the three others shows one of the places any belongs and uses it correctly. "There was hardly any light left in the reading room." follows hardly, which is almost a negative and pulls any after it in the same way not does. "I doubt whether there is any tape left in that box." follows an expression of doubt. And "If you find any old records in the attic, keep them for the club." follows if, the fourth of the triggers. Polarity, not quantity, is what decides between the two words.

questions.prompt: In 1995 a music lover in Le Kef could buy a record in exactly one shop in the whole town, and that shop has since closed. Speaking of those days he says: "If you wanted a record, you could not find it ___ else." Which word fills the gap?

options.text: nowhere
somewhere
nothing
anywhere

questions.explanation: "anywhere" is the word: the verb is already negative, could not, so the compound after it belongs to the any- series, and could not find it anywhere else is the ordinary way of saying it. "nowhere" would put the negative in the sentence a second time; English allows you could find it nowhere else, with an affirmative verb, but not both marks together. "somewhere" belongs to affirmative statements and reverses his meaning entirely. And "nothing" is from the right series in the wrong column: it names a thing, not a place, and the sentence needs a word that answers where.
